slides: Let's continue with the lines inside a regular polygon.

slides.say: Now the diagonals of a regular polygon. Here's a regular pentagon. Let's take one corner and draw both diagonals from it. From one corner of a pentagon, that's all we can draw.

The diagonals cut the corner's angle into three angles. And these three angles are equal. Why? Remember, every regular polygon fits in a circle. So each small angle has its corner on the circle. It's an inscribed angle.
at: every regular polygon fits in a circle

slides.say: Each small angle intercepts the arc under one side of the pentagon. All the sides are equal, so these arcs are equal too. And inscribed angles on equal arcs are equal. So the three angles are equal.
The whole angle is one hundred eight, so each one is one hundred eight divided by three. Ninety divided by three is thirty, and eighteen divided by three is six. So each angle is thirty-six.
at: one hundred eight divided by three

slides.say: It's the same in a regular hexagon. From one corner we can draw three diagonals. They cut the angle of one hundred twenty into four equal angles. One hundred twenty divided by four is thirty.
at: the same in a regular hexagon
One hundred twenty divided by four

slides.say: Let's look at those small angles again. In the regular pentagon, each one was thirty-six. In the regular hexagon, each one was thirty. And there's a pattern here. Thirty-six is one hundred eighty divided by five. And thirty is one hundred eighty divided by six.
at: Thirty-six is one hundred eighty divided by five
thirty is one hundred eighty divided by six

slides.say: Why one hundred eighty divided by n? Because each small angle is an inscribed angle, and it intercepts the arc under one side. The central angle on that same arc is three hundred sixty divided by n. In the pentagon, that's seventy-two. And an inscribed angle is half of the central angle on the same arc. So each small angle is half of three hundred sixty over n. That's one hundred eighty over n, and in the pentagon, half of seventy-two is thirty-six.
at: The central angle on that same arc
is three hundred sixty divided by n
That's one hundred eighty over n

slides.say: So every side adds one hundred eighty over n to an angle like this. Here's the rule. Take an angle whose corner is a corner of the polygon, and whose two arms go through two other corners. Count the sides between the two arms, on the far side from the corner. The angle is that number of sides, times one hundred eighty over n.

Let's check it on the whole angle of the pentagon. Its arms are the two sides at the corner. Between them, on the far side, there are three sides. Three times thirty-six is one hundred eight. That's exactly the pentagon's angle, like we found before.
at: Between them, on the far side

slides.say: This works only in a regular polygon, because only there are all the sides equal, so all their arcs are equal. And the angle's corner must be a corner of the polygon, and both arms must go through corners too. Only then is it an inscribed angle on those arcs.
at: This works only in a regular polygon

slides.say: Let's use it. Here's a regular polygon with ten sides, A to J. From corner A, we draw two diagonals, to D and to G. What is the angle alpha between them?
at: Here's a regular polygon with ten sides

slides.say: First, what one side adds. One hundred eighty divided by ten is eighteen. So every side between the arms adds eighteen degrees.
at: One hundred eighty divided by ten

slides.say: Now we count the sides between the arms, from D to G. They are D E, E F and F G. That's three sides. So alpha is three times eighteen, which is fifty-four.
at: D E, E F and F G
